summary: This Trinidad and Tobago Weather Center page explains the dry season, an annual period of below-average rainfall that typically runs from January or February to late May or June. It describes the atmospheric criteria the Trinidad and Tobago Meteorological Service uses to declare the season's start, the impacts such as heat, fires, water scarcity and mosquito breeding, and recommended public preparedness steps.
one_line: Explains Trinidad and Tobago's annual dry season: its timing, atmospheric causes, impacts and recommended water, heat and fire preparedness.
key_facts: The dry season in Trinidad and Tobago is an annual period where lower than average rainfall occurs.
The dry season can start as early as the beginning of January to as late as February and continue until late May or into June.
The Trinidad and Tobago Meteorological Service states the dry season occurs during January to May and is characterized by a tropical maritime climate.
Late May and December are considered transitional periods to the wet and dry seasons, respectively.
There is no fixed date for the beginning of the dry season; the Trinidad and Tobago Meteorological Service officially declares its start once climatic criteria are met.
During the dry season, the North Atlantic Subtropical High-Pressure System strengthens and expands toward the Caribbean; it is sometimes called the Bermuda-Azores High.
Typically the difference between pressure at the center of the North Atlantic Subtropical High and Trinidad is between 6 to 8 millibars.
In Trinidad a hot day is temperatures recorded greater than 34.0°C, while in Tobago a hot day is 32.0°C.
Hot Spell Alerts and Hot Spell Watches are issued only if there is risk of temperatures exceeding 34.0°C during the day and minimum nighttime temperatures above 24.0°C on at least 3-5 days.
Trade wind inversion caps shallow cumulus clouds from becoming taller during the dry season.
The dry season is never without rainfall, though rainfall events and occasionally thunderstorms are sporadic and increase during the transition months (December and May).
Drier conditions can increase the need to collect and store water in containers, which can increase breeding areas for mosquitoes.
Residents are advised to have a water backup plan that includes storing water to last 3-7 days.
Residents are advised to refrain from burning rubbish in grassy or forested areas during the dry season.
The page is an official-style resource and advises consulting the local meteorological office or disaster management office for official forecasts and warnings.
